subject: Archaeology
title: The Flood Tablet: Gilgamesh and the Bible
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Flood Tablet: Gilgamesh and the Bible.

hook.text: In 1872, George Smith found a clay tablet describing a great flood — and the story was older than the Bible by a thousand years.

buildup.text: Tablet XI of Gilgamesh describes Utnapishtim building a boat, loading animals, surviving a flood, and releasing a dove.

discovery.text: The parallels to Noah are unmistakable: divine warning, a boat, a flood, animals, a dove, and a landing on a mountain.

twist.text: The discovery shook Victorian England. If the Bible's flood story was borrowed from Babylon, what else was not original?

climax.text: The Daily Telegraph funded Smith's trip to Nineveh to find the missing piece — and incredibly, he found it.

punchline.text: A newspaper paid an archaeologist to find one tablet shard in Iraq's rubble.

quiz.question: Why did the Flood Tablet discovery shock Victorian England?
options: It proved that all ancient civilizations experienced the same flood
It showed the Bible's flood story was borrowed from a much older Babylonian tale
It contained a prediction of future floods that seemed to be coming true

details.summary: Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh describes a great flood sent by the gods, a man who builds a boat to save life, and the dove sent to find dry land. Its parallels to the biblical story of Noah sparked intense debate about the literary relationship between the texts.
details.whyItMatters: The Flood Tablet challenged the assumption that the Bible contained entirely original narratives. It opened scholarship on how ancient Near Eastern literature influenced biblical traditions and raised lasting theological questions.
takeaways: The Flood Tablet describes a flood story paralleling Noah's account
It was translated by George Smith in 1872 from Nineveh tablets
The discovery sparked lasting debate about biblical originality

faq.question: How similar are the Gilgamesh and Noah flood stories?
faq.answer: Remarkably similar. Both feature divine anger, one righteous man warned to build a boat, animals saved in pairs, a mountain landing, and birds sent to test for dry land. The Mesopotamian version is older by at least a thousand years.

faq.question: Does the Flood Tablet prove the Bible copied Gilgamesh?
faq.answer: Not directly. Scholars believe both draw from a shared Mesopotamian tradition of flood narratives. The biblical authors likely knew these older stories and adapted them within their own theological framework, just as many cultures reinterpret inherited myths.
